frames.narration: A client wants to update the row com.cnn.www, a Webtable row whose key is a reversed hostname. First it has to find out which tablet server holds that row. Its cache of tablet locations is empty.

The client follows the three-level hierarchy: a file in Chubby points to the root tablet, the root tablet points to the right METADATA tablet, and that tablet names the tablet server that holds the row range. That is three round trips, one of them to Chubby. The client caches the answer, so it will not need to do this again for this range.

messages.label: tablet server 17, via root and METADATA

frames.narration: The client sends the write straight to the tablet server. The master is not involved, which is why it stays lightly loaded. The server checks that the mutation is well formed and that the sender is allowed to write, by reading the list of permitted writers from a Chubby file, almost always already in its cache.

The server appends the mutation to its commit log in GFS first, using group commit so that many small writes share a disk write. Only then does it put the update into the memtable, a sorted buffer in memory. If the server crashes now, the log has what the memtable had.

messages.label: append to the commit log (group commit)

frames.narration: Later, a read for the same row arrives. The server answers from a merged view of the memtable and the SSTables, the immutable sorted files in GFS. A Bloom filter for each SSTable tells it which files might hold the row, so it skips the rest, and a block cache serves a recently used block without a disk read.

messages.label: check files whose Bloom filter says maybe

frames.narration: When the memtable reaches its size limit, a minor compaction freezes it and writes it to GFS as a new SSTable, and a fresh memtable takes over. Reads and writes continue throughout. Every flush adds a file, so in the background a merging compaction combines a few files into one, and occasionally a major compaction rewrites all of them into a single file with no deleted data in it.

If this tablet server dies, the master gives its tablets to other servers. The commit log, which mixes the mutations of all the failed server's tablets, is sorted by table, row and sequence number, in 64 MB pieces in parallel, so that each new server can read just its own tablets' mutations with one seek and replay them to rebuild the memtable. The tablets are serving again within moments.

messages.label: sorted log: replay only this tablet's entries
